# Lotka-Volterra

`lotka-volterra`

## Introduction

The Lotka-Volterra model is the textbook model of predators and prey. Rabbits
eat grass and breed; foxes eat rabbits and breed; foxes die. With more rabbits
the foxes thrive, with more foxes the rabbits dwindle, then the starving foxes
die off and the rabbits recover. The two populations rise and fall in turn,
the fox peak trailing the rabbit peak. The equations are older than artificial
chemistry: Alfred Lotka derived them from the theory of autocatalytic chemical
reactions (1910) and applied them to plants and herbivores (1920), and Vito
Volterra found them independently (1926) while explaining fish-catch data from
the Adriatic.

Banzhaf and Yamamoto use the model to show that ecology can be written as
chemistry (book §7.2.8, "Interacting Species"). Each animal is a molecule and
each event of its life is a reaction: a rabbit meeting grass becomes two
rabbits, a fox meeting a rabbit becomes two foxes, a fox disappears. Written
this way, the familiar predator-prey equations are just the mass-action rate
equations of three reactions. The book then gives the general form for any
number of species, in which each pair can be predator and prey, competitors,
or partners. The book notes that the Lotka-Volterra equation is "typically
used to study foodwebs in ecosystems".

The book's second point is about the reactor. Integrated as differential
equations, the populations circle forever. Simulated molecule by molecule in a
small volume, the same three reactions give erratic oscillations and "frequent
extinctions". The book's figure 7.5 sets the two side by side. So this small
chemistry shows that the choice of reactor algorithm is part of the model.

It is a simulation model with a fixed set of species: a few written-down
reactions, nothing constructive. Its closest neighbours are in the same
chapter. The [replicator equation](replicator-equation.md) is the same kind of
pairwise-interaction model from evolutionary game theory, and the book says the
two are equivalent: n Lotka-Volterra species correspond to a replicator system
of n + 1 strategies. The replicator model keeps the population size fixed by a
dilution flow, while Lotka-Volterra populations are unbounded.
[Logistic growth](logistic-chemistry.md) is the one-species version of the
same point about deterministic and stochastic readings.
[Random catalytic networks](random-catalytic-networks.md) contain both
equations as special cases. [Ecolab](ecolab.md) (book §8.2.3) runs the general
Lotka-Volterra equation with mutating species, so the set of species changes
over time.

## How it works

### Three reactions for rabbits and foxes

In the book's example, `X` is the prey (rabbits), `Y` the predator (foxes) and
`G` the grass:

```
X + G --ka--> 2 X + G      a rabbit eats grass and reproduces
Y + X --kb--> 2 Y          a fox eats a rabbit and reproduces
Y     --kc--> (nothing)    a fox dies
```

`ka`, `kb` and `kc` are rate constants. The grass sits on both sides of the
first reaction: it is a *catalyst*, needed but not used up, and the book
assumes its amount stays constant. Under the *law of mass action* a reaction
runs at a speed equal to its rate constant times the product of its reactants'
concentrations. Summing each species' gains and losses gives the book's
equations 7.28 and 7.29, with `x` and `y` the concentrations of rabbits and
foxes and `g0` the fixed amount of grass:

```
dx/dt = ka·g0·x − kb·y·x
dy/dt = kb·y·x − kc·y
```

Both rates vanish at the fixed point `x = kc/kb`, `y = ka·g0/kb`. Around it the
populations cycle.

Chemart folds the constant grass into the first rate: `X + G -> 2 X + G` with
rate `ka` becomes `X -> 2 X` with rate `ka·g0`, which gives the same equations.
The default network, with the book's values `ka = kb = kc = 1` and `g0 = 1`,
is printed under "Using it in Chemart" below: `X1` is the rabbit and `X2` the
fox.

### Walking through a cycle

Start, as the book's figure does, with 5 units of rabbits and 2 of foxes, well
away from the fixed point `(1, 1)`. Integrating the three generated reactions
(the script is under "Using it" below) gives:

```
X1 from 0.025 to 5.380; X2 from 0.025 to 5.380
X1 peaks at t = [9.16, 18.49, 27.81, 37.14]
V = x - ln x + y - ln y: start 4.697415, end 4.697415
```

With `x` = 5 and `y` = 2, foxes are born at a rate `x·y = 10` and die at
`y = 2`, so they multiply quickly and eat the rabbits down. By `t ≈ 2.5` the
rabbits have fallen to 0.025 units, a two-hundredth of where they started.
Then the foxes starve, the few rabbits left recover, and the cycle repeats with
a period of about 9.3 time units, each lap an exact copy of the last.

The cycle does not decay or grow because the system conserves a quantity. With
all constants 1 it is `V = x − ln x + y − ln y` (the third output line), and
each orbit is a curve of constant `V`. The size of the swing is therefore set
by the starting point, not by the parameters. Starting at `(1.5, 1)` the
rabbits swing only between 0.626 and 1.5; starting at `(1, 1)` nothing moves.

### The same reactions, one molecule at a time

The stochastic simulation algorithm (SSA) of Gillespie treats the reactions as
random events between whole molecules. The volume enters through a scale
factor, written here `omega` (Avogadro's number times the volume): the number
of molecules in one unit of concentration. The book's figure uses a volume
with `omega = 20`, so the start is 100 rabbits and 40 foxes. At the bottom of
the deterministic cycle the rabbits would be at 0.025 × 20 = 0.5 molecules.
A population of whole molecules cannot follow that. Once the last rabbit is
eaten, the rabbits are gone for good, and the foxes die out after them. Once
the last fox dies, the rabbits grow without limit, since nothing else checks
them. Extinction is final because every reaction needs a molecule of the
species it makes.

### The general form

The book's equation 7.30 extends this to n species:

```
dx_i/dt = x_i · (r_i + Σ_j b_ij · x_j)
```

`r_i` is species i's own growth rate (positive) or death rate (negative).
`b_ij` says what species j does to species i: zero for no effect, positive
if j helps i grow, negative if j "eats" i. The pair of signs names the
relationship: both positive is *mutualism*, both negative is *competition*,
one of each is *antagonism*. `b_ij = 1` with `b_ji = −1` is the predator-prey
case, i the predator. The diagonal entry `b_ii` is how members of one species
help or hinder each other, for example crowding.

Chemart turns each term into the mass-action reaction with the same
contribution to the equations:

| term | reaction | rate |
|---|---|---|
| `r_i > 0` | `X_i -> 2 X_i` | `r_i` |
| `r_i < 0` | `X_i -> ∅` | `−r_i` |
| `b_ii > 0` | `2 X_i -> 3 X_i` | `b_ii` |
| `b_ii < 0` | `2 X_i -> X_i` | `−b_ii` |
| `b_ij > 0` | `X_i + X_j -> 2 X_i + X_j` (j is a catalyst) | `b_ij` |
| `b_ij < 0` | `X_i + X_j -> X_j` (j destroys i) | `−b_ij` |
| `b_ij = −b_ji > 0` | `X_i + X_j -> 2 X_i` (i eats j) | `b_ij` |

The last row merges two terms: when the predator gains exactly what the prey
loses, the two reactions become one, the book's fox-eats-rabbit reaction.
With any other pair of values the two terms stay separate reactions. The
`b_ij > 0` and `b_ij < 0` rows are the reactions the book uses for the
replicator equation (its reactions 7.22 and 7.23).

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*explicit* — listed up front). n interacting species X_1..X_n; classically prey X1 and predator X2

**R — reactions** (*explicit* — listed reaction by reaction; molecules per reaction: 1, 2). X + G --ka--&gt; 2X + G ; Y + X --kb--&gt; 2Y ; Y --kc--&gt; (nothing)

general form x_i' = x_i (r_i + sum_j b_ij x_j)

**A — reactor**: `ode` (deterministic rate equations: concentrations change continuously in time); or `ssa` (stochastic simulation (Gillespie): individual reaction events happen at random times).

*How the population is bounded:* none

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("lotka-volterra", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
lotka-volterra: 2 species, 3 reactions, status=complete
provides: catalysts, initial-state, rate-constants, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
X1 -> 2 X1  [mass-action k=1.0]
X2 -> ∅  [mass-action k=1.0]
X2 + X1 -> 2 X2  [mass-action k=1.0]
```

The default call above is the book's figure 7.5 system: `r = [1, −1]` (rabbits
grow at `ka·g0 = 1`, foxes die at `kc = 1`), the predator-prey matrix
`B = [[0, −1], [1, 0]]` (`b_12 = −1`: the fox eats the rabbit; `b_21 = 1`: the
fox gains), and `x0 = [5, 2]`. Species are named `X1`, `X2`, ... in the order
of `r`; `net.initial_state` holds `x0`, and `net.extras` is empty. The network
involves no randomness, so `seed` changes nothing.

Chemart builds the network; it does not simulate it. The runs on this page use
short scripts of your own.

#### The deterministic cycle

This script integrates the generated network under mass action and produced
the output shown under "Walking through a cycle". It takes about a second.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

import chemart


def simulate(net, t_end, n=4001):
    ids, R, P = net.matrices()
    R = R.toarray()
    S = (P.toarray() - R).astype(float)
    k = np.array([r.rate["k"] for r in net.reactions])
    x0 = np.array([net.initial_state[s] for s in ids])

    def f(t, x):
        return S @ (k * np.prod(x[:, None] ** R, axis=0))  # mass action

    t = np.linspace(0, t_end, n)
    sol = solve_ivp(f, (0, t_end), x0, t_eval=t, rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12)
    return t, dict(zip(ids, sol.y))


net = chemart.generate_network("lotka-volterra")
t, x = simulate(net, 40)
X1, X2 = x["X1"], x["X2"]
print(f"X1 from {X1.min():.3f} to {X1.max():.3f}; X2 from {X2.min():.3f} to {X2.max():.3f}")
peaks = [t[i] for i in range(1, len(t) - 1) if X1[i - 1] < X1[i] > X1[i + 1]]
print("X1 peaks at t =", [round(float(p), 2) for p in peaks])
V = X1 - np.log(X1) + X2 - np.log(X2)
print(f"V = x - ln x + y - ln y: start {V[0]:.6f}, end {V[-1]:.6f}")
```

Pass `x0=[1.5, 1.0]` for a smaller cycle, or `x0=[1.0, 1.0]` to sit at the
fixed point.

#### A stochastic run in a small volume

To reproduce the right half of figure 7.5, convert each rate constant `k` to a
stochastic constant `c` with `k_to_c` and run Gillespie's algorithm. Each run
below stops at `t = 200` or when a species dies out:

```python
from math import comb

import numpy as np

import chemart
from chemart.kinetics import k_to_c


def gillespie(net, omega, t_end, seed):
    """Stop at t_end or when a species dies out; return (t, counts)."""
    n = {s: round(c * omega) for s, c in net.initial_state.items()}
    c = [k_to_c(r.rate["k"], r.reactants, volume=omega, avogadro=1.0) for r in net.reactions]
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t = 0.0
    while t < t_end and all(n.values()):
        a = np.array([ci * np.prod([comb(n[s], m) for s, m in r.reactants.items()])
                      for ci, r in zip(c, net.reactions)])
        t += rng.exponential(1 / a.sum())
        r = net.reactions[rng.choice(len(a), p=a / a.sum())]
        for s, m in r.reactants.items():
            n[s] -= m
        for s, m in r.products.items():
            n[s] += m
    return t, n


net = chemart.generate_network("lotka-volterra")
c = [k_to_c(r.rate["k"], r.reactants, volume=20, avogadro=1.0) for r in net.reactions]
print("c:", c)
for omega in (20, 200):
    out = []
    for seed in range(10):
        t, n = gillespie(net, omega, 200, seed)
        gone = [s for s, v in n.items() if v == 0]
        out.append((round(t, 1), gone[0] if gone else "-"))
    print(f"omega={omega}:", out)
```

```
c: [1.0, 1.0, 0.05]
omega=20: [(1.2, 'X1'), (1.7, 'X1'), (2.8, 'X1'), (5.9, 'X2'), (1.1, 'X1'), (2.2, 'X1'), (1.6, 'X1'), (5.2, 'X2'), (1.6, 'X1'), (1.6, 'X1')]
omega=200: [(200.0, '-'), (1.9, 'X1'), (20.0, 'X2'), (13.2, 'X1'), (16.9, 'X2'), (13.2, 'X1'), (7.7, 'X2'), (10.7, 'X1'), (9.1, 'X2'), (72.5, 'X2')]
```

The constants match the book's caption: the predation reaction gets
`c = kb/omega = 0.05`, while the one-molecule reactions keep `c = k = 1`. The
book's `ca = 0.05` times its 20 grass molecules is the same growth rate 1 that
Chemart's folded reaction gets directly. In the book's volume (`omega = 20`)
every one of ten runs ended in extinction within six time units, before the
first deterministic cycle (9.3 time units) was complete: eight times the
rabbits went first, in the trough the ODE puts near `t = 2.5`, and twice the
foxes did. With ten times the molecules (`omega = 200`) most runs got through
at least one cycle, and one of ten lasted the full 200 time units. The script
takes about a minute, mostly for that surviving run; the time grows with
`omega` and with how long the populations survive.

#### More than two species

`r` sets the number of species, `B` must be square of the same size, and `x0`
gives one starting value per species. A food chain in which `X1` is eaten by
`X2`, which is eaten by `X3`:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("lotka-volterra", r=[1.0, -0.5, -0.5],
                               B=[[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, -1], [0, 1, 0]], x0=[1, 1, 1])
print(net.to_text())
```

```
X1 -> 2 X1  [mass-action k=1.0]
X2 -> ∅  [mass-action k=0.5]
X3 -> ∅  [mass-action k=0.5]
X2 + X1 -> 2 X2  [mass-action k=1.0]
X3 + X2 -> 2 X3  [mass-action k=1.0]
```

Two species competing for the same resource, each also limited by crowding
(negative diagonal), give separate reactions for every term:

```python
net = chemart.generate_network("lotka-volterra", r=[1.0, 1.0],
                               B=[[-1.0, -0.5], [-0.5, -1.0]], x0=[0.1, 0.2])
print(net.to_text())
```

```
X1 -> 2 X1  [mass-action k=1.0]
X2 -> 2 X2  [mass-action k=1.0]
2 X1 -> X1  [mass-action k=1.0]
2 X2 -> X2  [mass-action k=1.0]
X1 + X2 -> X2  [mass-action k=0.5]
X2 + X1 -> X1  [mass-action k=0.5]
```

Integrated with the `simulate` function above to `t = 50`, both settle at
0.6667, where they coexist.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `r` | `list` | `[1.0, -1.0]` | kinetic | spontaneous growth (&gt;0) or death (&lt;0) rate per species; its length sets n |
| `B` | `list` | `[[0.0, -1.0], [1.0, 0.0]]` | kinetic | interaction matrix b_ij: 0 none, &gt;0 j feeds i, &lt;0 j eats i; both &gt;0 mutualistic, both &lt;0 competitive, mixed antagonistic |
| `x0` | `list` | `[5.0, 2.0]` | population | initial concentrations |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "3 decisions"

    - The general form (eq. 7.30) is the parameterisation. Each term becomes the mass-action reaction with the same ODE contribution, and a predator-prey pair b_ij = -b_ji &gt; 0 becomes the single reaction X_i + X_j -&gt; 2 X_i (eq. 7.26).
    - Defaults are figure 7.5's predator-prey system (ka = kb = kc = 1, x0 = 5, y0 = 2, g0 = 1), with the constant grass G folded into r_1 = ka g0.
    - NAV is not a parameter: it sizes a stochastic simulation, not the network.

## Results

The book treats the Lotka-Volterra model as a worked example rather than as a
source of new findings, and summarises what is known about it.

**Sustained oscillations under the rate equations.** The book derives the
fixed point `x = kc/kb`, `y = ka·g0/kb` from equations 7.28–7.29 and states
that "a stability analysis reveals oscillations around the equilibrium",
shown in figure 7.5 (left) for `ka = kb = kc = 1`, `x0 = 5`, `y0 = 2`,
`g0 = 1`. Chemart reproduces this. Its test
(`tests/chemistries/test_w1_dynamics.py`,
`test_lotka_volterra_matches_book_reactions_and_conserves_invariant`) checks
that the default network is exactly the book's reactions 7.25–7.27 with the
grass folded in, and that after integrating to `t = 20` the quantity
`x − ln x + y − ln y` is unchanged to within 10⁻⁵, which means the orbit
neither spirals in nor out.

**Erratic oscillations and extinction in small volumes.** Figure 7.5 (right)
repeats the run with Gillespie's SSA in a volume holding 100 rabbits, 40 foxes
and 20 grass molecules at the start. The book reports that "in small
populations contingency coming from stochastic fluctuations causes erratic
oscillations and frequent extinctions". Chemart's network, with the book's
stochastic constants, gives extinction in all ten runs above, and survival
for longer as the volume grows. No test checks the stochastic behaviour, and
Chemart has no built-in SSA: the result depends on a script like the one
above. The book's figure could not be compared point by point, since the text
does not give its individual runs.

**Cyclic food chains, waves and clustering.** The book says Lotka-Volterra
models have been studied "in well-mixed and spatial scenarios, as well as
deterministic and stochastic settings", citing Andrews and Bray (2004),
Dobramysl and Täuber (2008) and Mobilia, Georgiev and Täuber (2007). It lists
generalisations with cyclic food chains, in which the predator of one species
is the prey of another, and with mutation, citing Abrams (2000), Frachebourg,
Krapivsky and Ben-Naim (1996), Rikvold (2007) and Szabó and Czárán (2001). The
behaviours it names are oscillations, explosion of prey populations,
extinction of both species, "waves of predators chasing preys" and clustering
of species. Chemart builds the well-mixed networks, including cyclic chains
through the matrix `B`. Waves and clustering need space, and this chemistry has
no spatial reactor, so Chemart does not reproduce them. It does not implement
mutation either; [Ecolab](ecolab.md) does.

**Equivalence with the replicator equation.** The book states, citing Nowak
(2006) and Stadler, Fontana and Miller (1993), that after a transformation of
parameters the n-species equation is equivalent to a replicator equation with
n + 1 strategies. Chemart does not implement or test this transformation.

**Later use in artificial chemistry.** In §8.2.3 the book describes Standish's
Ecolab, which runs the general equation 7.30 with mutating `r_i` and `b_ij`
and shows a power-law distribution of species lifetimes. That is a separate
entry, [Ecolab](ecolab.md).
